title: ASCII Format for Network Interchange
summary: Specifies using the standard seven-bit ASCII character code for exchanging text between computers on the ARPANET, over host-to-host connections. It reproduces the USA Standard Code for Information Interchange and notes that each host defines its own break characters. It later became an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 20 sets a common way to encode letters and symbols so messages sent between computers look the same on both ends.

questions: how is ascii encoded in a byte
subtitle: An early agreement to use seven-bit ASCII for exchanging text on the ARPANET, with each host defining its own line breaks.

tldr.problem: Computers on the network needed to agree on which number stands for which character so that text typed on one host reads the same on another.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 20 specifies using standard 7-bit ASCII embedded in an 8-bit byte with the high-order bit set to 0, over host-to-host connections. The code is USAS X3.4-1968. Each host defines its own break characters.
tldr.outcome: The agreement established a common text encoding for network interchange. RFC 20 is an Internet Standard.

facts.label: Code width
facts.value: 7 bits, in an 8-bit byte with the high-order bit 0

today: RFC 20 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 20 proposes using the standard 7-bit ASCII character code for network interchange. It is embedded in an 8-bit byte with the high-order bit always 0, and is used over host-to-host primary connections. The memo reproduces the code table from USAS X3.4-1968.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers need a shared alphabet. This memo says to use the standard ASCII code, putting each character in a single 8-bit unit with the extra bit always set to 0.

sections.title: The ASCII Code
sections.content: The standard code is 7 bits arranged in 8 columns and 16 rows. Characters are identified by column and row (e.g., 'K' is column 4, row 11, which is bit pattern 1 0 0 1 0 1 1 for bits b7 through b1). The notation ASCII or USASCII refers to the latest standard; the year may be appended to designate a specific issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter, number, or symbol is given a unique 7-bit number. The table shows exactly which number matches which character.

sections.title: Break Characters
sections.content: Break characters (line ending signals) are defined by the receiving remote host. For example, SRI uses the period character (., ASCII 2/14) as the end-of-line character, while UCLA uses carriage return (CR, ASCII 0/13).
sections.plainLanguage: While the letters are standardized, different computers at the time used different characters to mark the end of a line.

sections.title: Control and Graphic Characters
sections.content: The specification lists control characters (such as NUL, LF, CR, HT) and graphic characters, noting their meanings. It also clarifies that DEL is not strictly a control character in that sense.
sections.plainLanguage: The code includes both printable characters (like letters and spaces) and control characters (like line feed and carriage return) that tell devices what to do.

viz.caption: ASCII is 7 bits in an 8-bit byte (high bit 0)
